title: What an agent identity is made of
lede: An agent access key is the agent's whole identity: who it acts as, what is attached to it, and what it can reach. The workload-identity path is drawn as the design, not a tested flow.

nodes.label: Custodian
sub: the human the agent acts as

steps.title: Who the key acts as
steps.what: Every agent key has a custodian: the human it acts as. Policy is issued to them and the gateway log names them. A key can instead be owned by a NonHumanIdentity, which proves itself with a platform token and holds no static secret.
steps.why: If the custodian goes inactive, the key stops working. Pick someone who will stay.

steps.title: Selecting apps creates the grant
steps.what: When apps are selected on the key, Privilege creates a policy issued to the custodian and tied to this key. For MCP apps the grant can list individual tools.
steps.why: Selecting the app is the grant. Nothing else needs writing.

steps.title: What it can reach
steps.what: The key reaches the apps and models its grant covers, and the grant decides which tools are visible.
steps.why: Tools not in the grant are hidden and refused.

steps.title: Scopes and limits
steps.what: Scopes (llm, mcp, a2a) set which gateway surfaces the key can use. Limits cap models, requests and tokens per minute, budget and expiry.
steps.why: Give only the scopes the agent uses. A three-scope key is one secret that reaches models, tools and agents.

steps.title: The guardrail
steps.what: AI Guard is configured on the key, not on the app. It is the only screen on agent-to-agent calls.
steps.why: Defaults mostly alert rather than block, so thresholds are set on purpose.
